chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Sayf, from Mansur, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

If a man buys a sacrificial animal while believing it to be fat, it is sufficient for him even if it turns out not to be fat. And if a man buys a sacrificial animal while believing it to be lean, and finds it to be fat, it is sufficient for him. But if he buys it while knowing it is lean, it is not sufficient for him.
And if one buys his sacrificial animal and then wishes to buy a fattier one, he should buy it and sell the first one if he wishes.
ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for a sacrificial animal to be valid if the buyer's assessment of its quality was incorrect?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the principle of 'al-zann' (presumption) in fiqh, establishing that the validity of the sacrifice depends on the buyer's subjective belief at the time of purchase rather than objective reality, provided there was no prior knowledge of defect. It highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on the buyer's intent and awareness, distinguishing between mere assumption and definite knowledge of the animal's condition. The permission to exchange the animal for a superior one underscores the recommendation of offering the best possible sacrifice within one's means.
